summary: UCLA-NMC reports on writing a program that stores files on UCSB's Simple Minded File System, and what they learned. They want features from UCSB's approach, such as retrieving files in sized chunks, included in the network-wide File Transfer Protocol.

eli5.summary: After trying to store files on another school's computer, the writers share lessons and say what the standard file-sending rules should copy.

subtitle: What UCLA learned writing a program to store files at UCSB, and what they want in the network-wide file transfer protocol.

tldr.problem: UCLA-NMC built a program to store files at UCSB's Simple Minded File System (SMFS) and found both useful ideas and gaps that bear on the planned network-wide File Transfer Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what to copy from the UCSB protocol: retrieving files in requested-size chunks, one request with one response, and mandatory passwords. It also asks for a way to list stored files, and an appendix documents the FXFER program.
tldr.outcome: It is an experience report meant to stimulate discussion. The RFC lists the status as Unknown, and it updates RFC 122.

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown and it is not obsoleted. It updates RFC 122. It records early file transfer experience between UCLA and UCSB.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
UCLA-NMC finished a program that uses UCSB's storage capability through their Simple Minded File System (SMFS), described in RFC 122. The authors say they learned several things that apply to a network-wide File Transfer Protocol, and they want to stimulate further discussion.

They found things in the UCSB protocol that they would like in the network-wide protocol, and things in the proposed network protocol that the UCSB protocol lacks.
sections.eli5: The writers tried a real file-storing service, so now they can say from experience what a good sharing system should copy.

sections.title: What UCSB Got Right
sections.content:
In UCSB's retrieval procedure the user gives a bit count of how much to fetch in the current request. Successive RTF commands return successive pieces of the file, and the SPF command skips over portions. The authors like being able to size the "chunks" and reach any part of a file without fetching all of it. Their user programs become easier to write because the program always knows what to expect.

They also favour a one request, one response protocol. Each reply to an RTF shows the server is still listening, and defaulting keeps requests small, so overall transfer rate does not suffer much on significant transfers. They found UCSB's mandatory password scheme easy to use and expect any server site advertising file storage to require passwords (see RFC 238).
sections.eli5: Asking for a file one bite at a time, and getting an answer after every ask, means you always know what is coming and that someone is listening.

sections.title: What Was Missing
sections.content:
Soon after starting to use SMFS the authors found a serious gap: there is no way to ask "what files do I have there?" The author suspects some files are already stored there that were forgotten.

They argue a server should supply a nicely formatted character string describing the files stored for a given password or user, including details such as date created and size. They end by noting UCSB is providing the SEX system with useful out-of-line on-line storage, and hope for a widely accepted file transfer protocol implemented at many server sites.
sections.eli5: The one big missing piece was a way to ask the storage shelf for a list of everything you put there.

sections.title: Appendix: The FXFER Program
sections.content:
Appendix A describes FXFER, a re-entrant program written in Symbol that sends and receives files at UCSB using SMFS. Files are kept in a paged format, so a file Master lists as n pages takes 2048 n bytes at UCSB. The user's sign-on initials serve as both the access and modification passwords.

Commands include PF (send a file to UCSB), GF (retrieve one), DF (delete one), RN (rename, not yet implemented), ST (status) and X (exit). PA and NP raise and reset the level of trace output.
sections.eli5: The appendix is the instruction card for the program: one short command to put a file away, one to get it back, one to delete it.

references.text: White, J., Network Specifications for UCSB's Simple-Minded File System, RFC 122.
